chapterTitle: Warnings From the Wilderness — The Way of Escape, the Table of the Lord, and the Glory of God
themeTitle: “Let Him Who Thinks He Stands Be Careful That He Doesn’t Fall”

scripture.text: Now I would not have you ignorant, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea;
scripture.understanding: Paul turns from the athlete who might be disqualified (9:27) to a whole nation that was. “I would not have you ἀγνοέω — ignorant.” And notice he calls Israel “our fathers” — to a largely Gentile church. In Christ, the Corinthians have been grafted into Israel's story. Then the word “all” begins: all under the νεφέλη, the cloud of God's presence; all through the θάλασσα, the Red Sea. Every one of them experienced God's deliverance.

scripture.text: and were all baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea;
scripture.understanding: “All baptized into Moses.” Paul sees the Red Sea crossing as a kind of baptism: passing through water, under the cloud, into a new identity as Moses' people. Corinthian believers had been baptized into Christ and thought that guaranteed their safety whatever they did. Paul says: Israel had a baptism too.

scripture.text: and all ate the same spiritual food;
scripture.understanding: “All ate the same spiritual food” — the manna, bread from heaven. Πνευματικός here means given by the Spirit, supernatural in origin, and perhaps pointing beyond itself. Jesus would later say that He is the true bread from heaven (John 6:32–35). The Corinthians had the Lord's Supper. Israel had the manna.

scripture.text: and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank of a spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ.
scripture.understanding: “All drank the same spiritual drink” — water from the rock (Exodus 17; Numbers 20). Then a remarkable phrase: “a spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ.” Later Jewish tradition told of a rock or well that travelled with Israel through the wilderness, and a form of that story is already found in a first-century Jewish writing. Paul's point goes deeper than the legend: the One who sustained Israel was the pre-existent Christ Himself. He was present with His people long before Bethlehem.

scripture.text: However with most of them, God was not well pleased, for they were overthrown in the wilderness.
scripture.understanding: Then the shock. “With most of them, God was not well pleased” — the understatement is deliberate. Of the adult generation that left Egypt, only Joshua and Caleb entered the land. They were καταστρώννυμι — strewn, scattered like corpses — across the ἔρημος, the wilderness. Every privilege, and most of them died outside the promise.

scripture.text: Now these things were our examples, to the intent we should not lust after evil things, as they also lusted.
scripture.understanding: Ταῦτα δὲ τύποι — these things became τύποι, types, patterns, examples. A τύπος was the mark left by a blow, a stamp impressed in wax. Israel's history is stamped with lessons for us. The first and root warning: not to be ἐπιθυμηταί — cravers — of evil, as they craved. Every sin that follows begins with desire.

scripture.text: Don’t be idolaters, as some of them were. As it is written, “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play.”
scripture.understanding: Warning one: idolatry. Paul quotes Exodus 32:6 from the golden calf story: the people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to παίζω — to play, to revel. The word suggests dancing and celebration that slid into sexual immorality. Notice: eating and drinking in the presence of an idol. That is exactly what the strong in Corinth were doing at temple meals.

scripture.text: Let us not commit sexual immorality, as some of them committed, and in one day twenty-three thousand fell.
scripture.understanding: Warning two: sexual immorality. The background is Numbers 25, where Israelite men were drawn into sexual immorality with Moabite women and into the worship of Baal of Peor. Numbers 25:9 gives the number who died in the plague as 24,000; Paul says 23,000 “in one day.” Paul may be citing the number who fell on the single day, or rounding; the slight difference does not touch his point. Idolatry and sexual sin went together in the wilderness, and they went together in Corinth's temples.

scripture.text: Let us not test Christ, as some of them tested, and perished by the serpents.
scripture.understanding: Warning three: testing the Lord. Ἐκπειράζω — to put to the test thoroughly, to push to see how far you can go. In Numbers 21 the people complained against God and Moses, and fiery serpents came among them. Many manuscripts read “test Christ”; others read “the Lord.” If “Christ” is original, as many think, it is another identification of Israel's God with Jesus. The strong in Corinth were testing God by walking right up to the edge of idolatry.

scripture.text: Don’t grumble, as some of them also grumbled, and perished by the destroyer.
scripture.understanding: Warning four: grumbling. Γογγύζω is an onomatopoeic word, the sound of muttering. Israel grumbled constantly in the wilderness (Numbers 14; 16:41). The ὀλοθρευτής, the destroyer, recalls the destroying angel of Passover (Exodus 12:23). Grumbling sounds small. In Scripture it is treated as a symptom of unbelief.

scripture.text: Now all these things happened to them by way of example, and they were written for our admonition, on whom the ends of the ages have come.
scripture.understanding: All of this happened τυπικῶς — as a pattern — and was written down πρὸς νουθεσίαν ἡμῶν, for our warning, our admonition. And we are the people “on whom the τέλη of the ages have come.” The ends of the ages have arrived; the climax of history is now. That raises the stakes, not lowers them.

scripture.text: Therefore let him who thinks he stands be careful that he doesn’t fall.
scripture.understanding: The application in one sentence. “Let him who thinks he ἵστημι — stands — be careful that he doesn’t πίπτω — fall.” The strong in Corinth thought they were standing firm because of their knowledge and their sacraments. The greatest danger in the Christian life is not weakness but overconfidence.

scripture.text: No temptation has taken you except what is common to man. God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted above what you are able, but will with the temptation also make the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it.
scripture.understanding: One of the most loved promises in the Bible, and it comes in the middle of a warning. Πειρασμός — testing, temptation, trial. No temptation has seized you except what is ἀνθρώπινος — human, common to everyone. You are not uniquely tempted. Then: “God is faithful” (as in 1:9). He will not ἐάω — permit — you to be tempted beyond your ability, and with the temptation He will also make the ἔκβασις — the way out, the exit, a mountain pass out of a valley — so that you may be able ὑποφέρω — to bear up under it. The promise is not that you will never be tempted. It is that there will always be a door, and God will put it there.

scripture.text: Therefore, my beloved, flee from idolatry.
scripture.understanding: “Therefore” — because God provides a way of escape — “flee from εἰδωλολατρία.” The way of escape from idolatry is not to stand near it and resist; it is to run. Paul uses the same verb as 6:18 for sexual immorality: φεύγετε. And he calls them “my beloved” — the warning is from a father's heart.

scripture.text: I speak as to wise men. Judge what I say.
scripture.understanding: Paul appeals to their own judgment: “I speak as to φρόνιμοι — sensible people. κρίνω — judge for yourselves.” There may be a trace of irony; they prided themselves on their wisdom. But it is also respect: he wants them to see the logic, not just obey the rule.

scripture.text: The cup of blessing which we bless, isn’t it a sharing of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, isn’t it a sharing of the body of Christ?
scripture.understanding: “The cup of blessing which we bless” — a phrase very probably drawn from the Jewish meal liturgy, where the cup over which a thanksgiving was said after the meal was called the cup of blessing; at Passover it was the third cup. Is it not a κοινωνία, a sharing, a participation, in the blood of Christ? The bread we κλάω, break — is it not a participation in His body? The Lord's Supper is not just a memorial meal. It is communion — a real sharing in Christ.

scripture.text: Because there is one loaf of bread, we, who are many, are one body; for we all partake of the one loaf of bread.
scripture.understanding: One ἄρτος — one loaf — so we, who are many, are one body, because we all μετέχω, partake, of the one loaf. The picture is a single loaf of bread broken and shared around the room. Every person eating from it is joined to the others. This is why division at the Lord's Table (chapter 11) is so serious.

scripture.text: Consider Israel according to the flesh. Don’t those who eat the sacrifices participate in the altar?
scripture.understanding: Paul points to Israel's sacrificial system. Those who ate the sacrifices were κοινωνοί τοῦ θυσιαστηρίου — partners with the altar. To eat a sacrificial meal was to share in the worship it expressed. Eating is never just eating when it happens at an altar.

scripture.text: What am I saying then? That a thing sacrificed to idols is anything, or that an idol is anything?
scripture.understanding: Paul anticipates the strong's objection: are you saying an idol is real after all? No. He has already said in 8:4 that an idol is nothing. The meat is just meat. The statue is just stone. But that is not the whole truth, as the next verse shows.

scripture.text: But I say that the things which the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons, and not to God, and I don’t desire that you would have fellowship with demons.
scripture.understanding: The other half of the truth: what pagans sacrifice, they sacrifice δαιμονίοις — to demons — and not to God. Paul is echoing Deuteronomy 32:17. The idol is nothing, but behind it are real spiritual powers that receive the worship. And Paul does not want them to become κοινωνοί τῶν δαιμονίων — partners with demons. The theology of the strong was half right, and the missing half was deadly.

scripture.text: You can’t both drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You can’t both partake of the table of the Lord, and of the table of demons.
scripture.understanding: Two cups, two tables, and you cannot have both. The τράπεζα κυρίου, the table of the Lord, and the τράπεζα δαιμονίων, the table of demons. In the ancient world, invitations to temple banquets sometimes read “to dine at the table of the lord Serapis.” Paul uses the same language. You cannot sit at both tables. Exclusive loyalty is the nature of covenant.

scripture.text: Or do we provoke the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than he?
scripture.understanding: Two sharp questions echoing Deuteronomy 32:21, where God says Israel provoked Him to jealousy with what is not God. Do we παραζηλόω — provoke — the Lord to jealousy? Are we ἰσχυρότεροι — stronger — than He is? A direct jab at the “strong.” If you think your strength allows you to flirt with idolatry, are you stronger than God?

scripture.text: “All things are lawful for me,” but not all things are profitable. “All things are lawful for me,” but not all things build up.
scripture.understanding: The Corinthian slogan again (as in 6:12): “All things are lawful for me.” Paul's two answers now are not all things συμφέρω — benefit — and not all things οἰκοδομέω — build up. In chapter 6 the test was, will it master me? Here the test is, will it help others? The question shifts from self to neighbour.

scripture.text: Let no one seek his own, but each one his neighbor’s good.
scripture.understanding: The principle beneath the whole discussion. Μηδεὶς τὸ ἑαυτοῦ ζητείτω — let no one seek his own — ἀλλὰ τὸ τοῦ ἑτέρου — but that of the other. Love does not ask what is good for me, but what is good for him. It is 13:5 in advance: love “doesn’t seek its own way.”

scripture.text: Whatever is sold in the butcher shop, eat, asking no question for the sake of conscience,
scripture.understanding: Now practical guidance. Meat sold in the μάκελλον — the provision market; a Latin inscription mentioning Corinth's macellum has been found — you may eat without asking questions for conscience' sake. Some of it would have come from temple sacrifices; much of it would not. Paul tells believers not to investigate. Once meat is in the market, it is just food.

scripture.text: for “the earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness.”
scripture.understanding: The reason, from Psalm 24:1, which Jewish families recited as a blessing before meals: “the earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness.” Everything belongs to God. Food is His gift, whatever pagans may have done with it. An idol cannot steal what God made.

scripture.text: But if one of those who don’t believe invites you to a meal, and you are inclined to go, eat whatever is set before you, asking no questions for the sake of conscience.
scripture.understanding: If an unbeliever invites you to dinner at his home and you want to go, go. Eat what is παρατίθημι — set before you — without asking questions. Paul is not telling believers to withdraw from social life with pagans. He wants them at those tables, as Jesus ate with sinners.

scripture.text: But if anyone says to you, “This was offered to idols,” don’t eat it for the sake of the one who told you, and for the sake of conscience. For “the earth is the Lord’s, and all its fullness.”
scripture.understanding: But if someone μηνύω — points out, discloses — “This was offered to idols,” then do not eat. Why? For the sake of the one who told you, and for conscience. Someone has drawn attention to the meat's religious meaning; now eating it would be a statement. (The repeated quotation of Psalm 24:1 at the end of this verse in the WEB is found in later manuscripts; the earliest omit it.)

scripture.text: Conscience, I say, not your own, but the other’s conscience. For why is my liberty judged by another conscience?
scripture.understanding: “Conscience, I say, not your own, but the other’s.” Your own conscience is clear; you know the idol is nothing. But the other person's conscience is now involved. Then a question in the voice of the strong: why should my freedom be judged by someone else's conscience? Paul's answer is in the next verses: it should not be judged — but it should be limited by love.

scripture.text: If I partake with thankfulness, why am I denounced for something I give thanks for?
scripture.understanding: “If I partake with χάρις — with thanks — why am I βλασφημέω — slandered — over something I give thanks for?” Paul defends the freedom to eat with gratitude. But he is also saying: why give someone the opportunity to speak evil of what I receive with thanks? Thanksgiving is the believer's way of eating, and it should not become an occasion for slander.

scripture.text: Whether therefore you eat, or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.
scripture.understanding: The great summary of the whole section, and one of the broadest commands in the New Testament. Eating, drinking, “or whatever you do” — πάντα εἰς δόξαν θεοῦ ποιεῖτε, do everything for the glory of God. The most ordinary acts of life — a meal, a drink — are to be done to make God's worth visible. There is no secular corner of a Christian's life.

scripture.text: Give no occasion for stumbling, either to Jews, or to Greeks, or to the assembly of God;
scripture.understanding: Ἀπρόσκοποι γίνεσθε — become people who cause no one to stumble. Three groups: Jews, Greeks, and the church of God. Paul's concern reaches outward to unbelievers of every background, and inward to fellow believers. Your freedom must not become a stumbling block for anyone.

scripture.text: even as I also please all men in all things, not seeking my own profit, but the profit of the many, that they may be saved.
scripture.understanding: Paul's own example closes the argument: “I please all men in all things” — not by compromising truth but by setting aside his own preferences. “Not seeking my own σύμφορον — profit, advantage — but the profit of the many, that they may be saved.” The goal of Christian freedom, like everything else, is the salvation of others. And 11:1 follows: “Be imitators of me, even as I also am of Christ.”

visualMeditations.title: Bones in the Wilderness
visualMeditations.image: Picture the people of Israel on the far shore of the Red Sea. Behind them, the water has closed over Pharaoh's army. Above them, the pillar of cloud. Every one of them — men, women, children — has walked through the sea on dry ground. Every morning, manna lies on the ground like frost. When they are thirsty, water pours from a rock. They have seen more miracles in a month than most people see in a lifetime. And now follow them forward forty years. Picture the trail they left across the Sinai desert: grave after grave, the bones of an entire generation scattered across the sand. Of all the adults who walked through the sea, only two — Joshua and Caleb — set foot in the promised land.
visualMeditations.meaning: Paul repeats the word “all” five times in four verses: all under the cloud, all through the sea, all baptized, all ate, all drank. Then: “with most of them, God was not well pleased.” The Corinthians thought their baptism and the Lord's Supper made them safe, whatever they did at the temple banquets. Paul says Israel had their own baptism and their own spiritual food and drink — and it did not save them from the consequences of idolatry, immorality, testing God and grumbling. Spiritual privilege is not the same as spiritual safety. Experiences of God's power are not a substitute for faithful obedience. Many have walked through the sea and died in the desert.

visualMeditations.title: The Mountain Pass
visualMeditations.image: Picture an army surrounded in a valley. Mountains rise on every side; the enemy holds every ridge. The soldiers are exhausted and the situation looks hopeless. Then a scout returns with news: there is a narrow pass through the mountains, hidden from the enemy's view. It is steep and difficult, but it is there. The army follows it, single file, and comes out on the other side. That narrow pass is the ἔκβασις of verse 13 — an exit, a way out of a closed place. The word was used for a passage out of a valley or a landing place out of the sea.
visualMeditations.meaning: This verse is not a promise that you will never face temptation, or that temptation will be easy. It is a promise about God's faithfulness inside temptation. First, your temptation is “common to man” — you are not uniquely cursed, and others have faced it and won. Second, God limits it: He will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able. Third, He provides the way out, together with the temptation itself — not after you have fallen, but with it. Fourth, the purpose is that you “may be able to endure it.” And notice what follows immediately: “Therefore, my beloved, flee from idolatry.” Sometimes the way of escape is not a mysterious rescue. It is a door you have to choose to run through.

visualMeditations.title: Two Tables
visualMeditations.image: On a Sunday evening in Corinth, a group of believers gather in a house. One loaf of bread is broken and passed from hand to hand; one cup is blessed and shared. They are remembering the Lord's death, and they are participating in His body and blood. Now picture the next evening, a mile away, in the dining hall of a pagan temple. An invitation card has gone out: “You are invited to dine at the table of the lord Serapis.” The meat comes from the altar. The meal begins with an offering to the god. And among the guests, reclining with a cup in his hand, is one of the believers from last night's gathering, telling himself that the idol is nothing.
visualMeditations.meaning: Paul agrees that the idol is nothing (v. 19). But he insists that something real is happening at that altar: “the things which the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons, and not to God” (v. 20). To eat a sacrificial meal is to become a κοινωνός, a partner, with whatever is being worshipped, just as eating the Lord's Supper is a κοινωνία in the body and blood of Christ. You cannot sit at both tables. Today the altars look different — but the principle is the same. Anything that receives the worship, loyalty and devotion that belong to God is an idol, and behind it are powers that are not neutral. Ask yourself what other tables you have been sitting at.

structure.label: Israel's Privileges (v. 1-4)
structure.body: All the Israelites were under the cloud, passed through the sea, were baptized into Moses, and ate and drank spiritual food and drink from the rock that was Christ.

structure.label: Israel's Fall and Its Lessons (v. 5-11)
structure.body: Yet most of them died in the wilderness because of craving evil, idolatry, sexual immorality, testing the Lord and grumbling — and these things were written as examples for us, on whom the ends of the ages have come.

structure.label: Warning and Promise (v. 12-13)
structure.body: Whoever thinks he stands should take care not to fall; but no temptation is beyond the ordinary, and God is faithful to provide the way of escape.

structure.label: Flee Idolatry: The Two Tables (v. 14-22)
structure.body: The Lord's Supper is a participation in Christ's body and blood and makes believers one body; pagan sacrifices are offered to demons, and believers cannot share both the Lord's table and the table of demons.

structure.label: Freedom, Conscience and the Glory of God (v. 23-33)
structure.body: Not everything lawful is beneficial or builds up; eat market meat and meals in unbelievers' homes freely, but abstain if someone points out it was offered to idols, for the sake of their conscience; do everything to the glory of God and seek the good of others so that they may be saved.

sections.heading: Baptized and Fed — and Still Overthrown
paragraphs: Chapter 10 follows directly from 9:27, where Paul said he disciplined his body so that he would not be disqualified. Now he gives an entire nation as an example of disqualification. The argument is aimed at the strong in Corinth, who apparently believed that their baptism and participation in the Lord's Supper made them spiritually secure, so they could attend temple banquets without danger. Paul says: look at Israel. “Our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea; and were all baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea; and all ate the same spiritual food; and all drank the same spiritual drink” (vv. 1–4). The repetition of “all” is deliberate — five times. Every single one of them experienced God's saving power and provision. And then verse 5: “However with most of them, God was not well pleased, for they were overthrown in the wilderness.”

Verse 4 contains one of the most striking statements about Christ in Paul's letters: “they drank of a spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ.” Later Jewish tradition developed a legend that the rock or well that gave water at the start of the wilderness journey travelled with Israel for forty years; an early form of this tradition appears in a Jewish work from about Paul's time known as Pseudo-Philo. Whether or not Paul has the legend in mind, his theological point is clear and bold: the One who sustained Israel in the wilderness was the pre-existent Christ. Moses' rock was a sign of a deeper reality. Jesus was present with His people long before His incarnation. And if Israel could sin against Christ in the wilderness and fall, so could the Corinthians.

Then come four specific warnings, each drawn from a wilderness story. Idolatry: the golden calf, where “the people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (v. 7, Exodus 32:6) — notice, eating and drinking at an idol feast, exactly the issue in Corinth. Sexual immorality: the incident at Baal-peor (Numbers 25), where idolatry and immorality went together, as they often did in Corinth's temples. (Numbers 25:9 says 24,000 died; Paul says 23,000 “in one day” — he may be counting those who fell on a single day, or using a round figure; the point is unaffected.) Testing the Lord: the complaint in Numbers 21 that brought the fiery serpents. Grumbling: the repeated murmuring that brought judgment (Numbers 14, 16). And then the purpose: “these things happened to them by way of example, and they were written for our admonition” (v. 11). The Old Testament is not ancient history to Paul. It is a warning written for the church.

sections.heading: Overconfidence and the Faithfulness of God
paragraphs: Verse 12 distils the warning into one sentence: “Therefore let him who thinks he stands be careful that he doesn’t fall.” The danger Paul is addressing is not weakness. It is overconfidence. The strong in Corinth were sure of their standing. They had knowledge, they had gifts, they had sacraments. And precisely because they were sure, they were walking into situations — temple banquets — that put them at risk of falling into idolatry. The most dangerous moment in the Christian life is often not when you feel weak, but when you feel strong enough not to need caution.

But Paul does not leave them with fear. Verse 13 is one of the great promises of Scripture, and its placement is important: it comes right in the middle of a warning about falling. “No temptation has taken you except what is common to man. God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted above what you are able, but will with the temptation also make the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it.” Four truths are packed into it. First, your temptation is ἀνθρώπινος — human, common. You are not the only one, and you are not facing something no one else has faced. Second, God is faithful — the same declaration as 1:9. Third, God sets limits: He will not permit temptation beyond your ability. Fourth, He provides the ἔκβασις, the way out, together with the temptation itself. The purpose is not to remove the trial but to enable you to “endure it” — to bear up under it and come through.

Then notice how verse 14 begins: “Therefore, my beloved, flee from idolatry.” The way of escape from temptation is very often to run. God makes the exit; you must take it. Many believers pray for deliverance while walking toward the very situation that tempts them, and then wonder why the escape did not appear. The Corinthians were praying, in effect, for protection while reclining at the table of an idol. Paul's answer is: God has given you a way out. It is the door. Use it. And James adds the necessary clarification: God does not tempt anyone; each one is tempted “when he is drawn away by his own lust, and enticed” (James 1:14). God tests to strengthen. Temptation comes from our desire and the enemy's design. But God is faithful in both.

sections.heading: The Lord's Table, the Demons' Table, and a Life for God's Glory
paragraphs: Verses 14 to 22 give Paul's decisive answer to the question of eating in pagan temples, which chapter 8 left open. In chapter 8 he argued from love for the weak brother. Here he argues from the nature of worship itself. The Lord's Supper is a κοινωνία — a sharing, a participation — in the blood and body of Christ (v. 16). The single loaf shared by all makes the many into one body (v. 17). And Israel's sacrificial meals made the eaters partners with the altar (v. 18). Eating at an altar is never just eating. It is participation in the worship that altar represents.

Then Paul completes the theology the strong had only half right. Yes, an idol is nothing (v. 19). But “the things which the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons, and not to God” (v. 20). He is echoing Deuteronomy 32:17, which says Israel “sacrificed to demons, not God.” Behind the empty statue are real spiritual powers that receive the worship given to it. To share in a temple meal is to become a κοινωνός of demons. “You can’t both drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You can’t both partake of the table of the Lord, and of the table of demons” (v. 21). Invitations survive from the ancient world that read, “to dine at the table of the lord Serapis” — Paul uses the same language. And he warns, echoing Deuteronomy 32:21, that to do so is to provoke the Lord to jealousy. “Are we stronger than he?”

Verses 23 to 33 then give practical guidance and a beautiful summary. Meat sold in the market can be eaten freely, without investigation, “for ‘the earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness’” (v. 26, Psalm 24:1). An unbeliever's dinner invitation can be accepted, and whatever is served eaten — unless someone points out that it was offered to idols, in which case abstain, for the sake of that person's conscience (vv. 27–29). This is not legalism; it is love. And then comes the principle that governs everything: “Whether therefore you eat, or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God” (v. 31). No part of life is spiritually neutral. A meal, a drink, a purchase, a conversation — all can make God's worth visible. And the measure is always others: “Give no occasion for stumbling, either to Jews, or to Greeks, or to the assembly of God; even as I also please all men in all things, not seeking my own profit, but the profit of the many, that they may be saved” (vv. 32–33).

ntConnection.heading: New Testament Connection
paragraphs: Paul's reading of the wilderness as a warning for the church is shared by the writer of Hebrews: “With whom was he displeased forty years? Wasn’t it with those who sinned, whose bodies fell in the wilderness? To whom did he swear that they wouldn’t enter into his rest, but to those who were disobedient? We see that they were not able to enter in because of unbelief” (Hebrews 3:17–19). And Paul states the principle behind his use of these stories in Romans: “For whatever things were written before were written for our learning, that through perseverance and through encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope” (Romans 15:4). The wilderness stories were written for us. And Jesus Himself saw His own death in one of them: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life” (John 3:14–15). The very episode Paul uses as a warning in verse 9 became, in Jesus' hands, a picture of salvation.

Paul's identification of Christ with the spiritual food and drink of Israel (vv. 3–4) is developed by Jesus in John's Gospel. When the crowd reminded Him that “Our fathers ate the manna in the wilderness,” Jesus replied, “it wasn’t Moses who gave you the bread out of heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread out of heaven... I am the bread of life. He who comes to me will not be hungry, and he who believes in me will never be thirsty” (John 6:31–35). And at the Feast of Tabernacles, which commemorated the wilderness journey, Jesus stood and cried, “If anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink!” (John 7:37). The rock that followed Israel has a name. And the Lord's Supper of verse 16 goes back to the night Jesus took bread and said, “Take, eat; this is my body,” and the cup, “this is my blood of the new covenant, which is poured out for many for the remission of sins” (Matthew 26:26, 28).

The promise of verse 13 finds its foundation in Christ's own experience. Hebrews says, “For we don’t have a high priest who can’t be touched with the feeling of our infirmities, but one who has been in all points tempted like we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15), and “in that he himself has suffered being tempted, he is able to help those who are tempted” (Hebrews 2:18). The faithful God who provides the way of escape does so through a Saviour who walked through every temptation Himself. Peter adds, “the Lord knows how to deliver the godly out of temptation” (2 Peter 2:9). And the command of verse 31 to do everything for God's glory echoes through the apostles' letters: “Whatever you do, in word or in deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father, through him” (Colossians 3:17); “that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 4:11).

lexicon.insight: Strong's: “a die (as struck), i.e. (by implication) a stamp or scar; by analogy, a shape, i.e. a statue, (figuratively) style or resemblance; specially, a sampler (‘type’), i.e. a model (for imitation) or instance (for warning).” The word comes from τύπτω, to strike — the same verb used in 8:12 for wounding a weak conscience. A τύπος is the mark left by a blow: the print of the nails in Jesus' hands (John 20:25), the impression stamped into a coin. Israel's experiences in the wilderness left a mark on history that serves as a pattern for the church. When Paul says these things are “examples,” he means they are stamped with lessons that apply directly to us.

Strong's: “a putting to proof (by experiment (of good), experience (of evil), solicitation, discipline or provocation); by implication, adversity.” The same word can mean a trial that tests and strengthens faith (James 1:2, 12) or an enticement to sin (Matthew 6:13). Both meanings may be present here: the situations in Corinth were both tests of loyalty and temptations to idolatry. The key truth is not that you can avoid πειρασμός — Jesus Himself faced it — but that God sets its limits and provides the way through. Every trial that comes into a believer's life has passed through the hands of a faithful God who has measured it against your strength.

Strong's: “an exit (literally or figuratively).” The word combines ἐκ (out of) and βαίνω (to go) — a going-out. It was used of a way out of a valley through the mountains, a landing place from the sea, or the outcome of a situation. Its only other New Testament use is Hebrews 13:7, of the “outcome” of the faith of former leaders. In 1 Corinthians 10:13 the article is significant: “the way of escape” — a specific exit designed for that specific temptation. God does not merely leave a door open somewhere; He makes the exit with the temptation. Your responsibility is to look for it and walk through it.

lexicon.strongs: G2842 (related noun, partner κοινωνός, koinōnós, G2844)
lexicon.insight: Strong's defines κοινωνία as “partnership, i.e. (literally) participation, or (social) intercourse,” and κοινωνός as “a sharer, i.e. associate.” This is the word from which the church gets “communion.” It appeared in 1:9 — called into the fellowship of His Son. Here it describes what happens at the Lord's Table: a real participation in the body and blood of Christ, and a real union with one another. Then Paul uses the related noun to describe what happens at a pagan altar: becoming partners with demons. Worship is never a spectator activity. Whatever you worship, you share in. That is why the table you sit at matters so much.

Strong's: “glory (as very apparent), in a wide application (literal or figurative, objective or subjective).” In the Old Testament, the Hebrew word for glory carries the sense of weight — God's heaviness, His substance and worth. In Greek, δόξα originally meant opinion or reputation and came to mean splendour and honour. To do something “to the glory of God” is to do it in a way that makes His worth visible and enhances His reputation in the eyes of others. Verse 31 extends that to eating and drinking — the most ordinary acts of life. There is nothing so small that it cannot either display or obscure the glory of God.

holySpiritRevelation.intro: The Spirit is dealing with three things in this chapter: the false security you have built on past experiences of God, the door of escape you keep walking past, and the other tables you have been sitting at.

items.title: You Walked Through the Sea — Will You Die in the Desert?
items.body: You have experienced God. You were baptized. You have felt His presence, received His provision, seen His answers to prayer. Perhaps you have even seen miracles. And the enemy wants you to believe that because of all that, you are safe whatever you do. Paul says: all of Israel walked through the sea, and most of them died in the wilderness. The Spirit is not trying to frighten you out of assurance. He is warning you out of presumption. Past experiences of God are not a licence for present compromise. Where have you been relying on yesterday's encounter while drifting today? “Let him who thinks he stands be careful that he doesn’t fall.”

items.title: The Door You Keep Walking Past
items.body: There is a temptation you keep falling into, and you have half-convinced yourself that it is beyond your power to resist. The Spirit wants you to hear verse 13 as a personal word: this temptation is common to man; God is faithful; He has not allowed it beyond what you can bear; and He has made a way of escape. The question is not whether the door exists. It is whether you are looking for it — and whether you are willing to run through it when you see it. Often the door appears early: a moment before the click, the drink, the conversation, the look. Ask the Spirit to show you where the door is in your specific temptation, and decide now to take it next time.

items.title: The Other Table
items.body: You sit at the Lord's Table. You take the bread and the cup. And there may be another table you have been sitting at too — something that receives the devotion, the trust, the loyalty that belong to God. Money. Approval. A relationship. Your career. Your image. An addiction. Something you go to for comfort and identity that is not Christ. You tell yourself it is nothing, just as the strong in Corinth did. But Paul says that behind idols are powers that are not neutral, and that you cannot sit at both tables. The Spirit is asking: what is the other table in your life? Will you get up from it?

audit.title: The Overconfidence Check
audit.body: Write down one area of your life where you feel spiritually secure enough to take risks other believers would avoid. Then ask honestly: is this freedom, or is it presumption? Am I standing — or do I only think I am standing? What would Israel's story say to me here?

audit.title: The Escape Check
audit.body: Name your most frequent temptation. Then trace backwards the last time you gave in to it. At what moment did the way of escape appear? What would it have looked like to take it? Write it down specifically — the time, the place, the choice.

audit.title: The Two-Tables Check
audit.body: List the three things that most compete with God for your trust, comfort and devotion. For each one, ask: if it were taken away, would I feel I had lost my security, my identity, or my joy? If so, it may have become a table you are sitting at alongside the Lord's.

practices.title: Mapping Your Exits
practices.body: Take a sheet of paper and write your top two temptations at the top. Under each, write down: (1) the situations, times or emotions that usually lead to it; (2) the earliest point at which you could turn away; (3) one specific action you will take at that point — a door you will walk through (for example: leave the room, call a friend, close the app, go for a walk, pray aloud). Write verse 13 at the bottom. Keep the page somewhere you will see it. Next time the temptation comes, look for the door you mapped, and take it. Then thank God for His faithfulness.

practices.title: An Ordinary Day to the Glory of God
practices.body: Choose one ordinary day this week. From the moment you wake up, deliberately do every task “to the glory of God” (v. 31) — eating, working, driving, cleaning, talking, resting. Before each activity, pause briefly and say, “Lord, let this show Your worth.” Before every meal, thank God aloud that the earth is the Lord's and its fullness. At the end of the day, write down what changed in how you did ordinary things, and where you noticed God in places you usually overlook.

prayerReflection: “Father, I thank You for every time You have brought me through the sea, covered me with Your cloud, and fed me with spiritual food and drink. Thank You that the Rock who followed Israel is Christ, and that He has followed me too. But Lord, I do not want to be one who walked through the sea and died in the desert. Forgive me for the times I have presumed on Your grace, relying on yesterday's experiences while drifting today. Keep me from craving evil, from idolatry, from sexual immorality, from testing You, and from grumbling. Let me learn from the examples You have written for me. Lord, I confess that I have thought I was standing when I was close to falling. Give me humility and holy caution. And thank You that You are faithful. Thank You that no temptation I face is beyond what is common to man, that You have measured every trial against my strength, and that You always make a way of escape. Open my eyes to see the door, and give me the courage to run through it. Jesus, I come to Your table. I share in Your body and blood. I renounce every other table — every idol that has taken the devotion that belongs to You. You alone are my Lord. And let me do everything — eating, drinking, working, resting, whatever I do — for the glory of God, seeking not my own good but the good of many, that they may be saved. In Your name, Amen.”

storyConnections.title: The Golden Calf
storyConnections.summary: While Moses was on the mountain receiving the law, the people grew impatient and asked Aaron to make them gods. He collected their gold earrings, cast a calf, and they declared it the god who brought them out of Egypt. Aaron built an altar and announced a feast to the LORD. The next morning they offered sacrifices, sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play. These were people who had seen the plagues, crossed the sea, eaten manna, and heard God's voice from the mountain only weeks before. And they turned to an idol and called it worship. Paul quotes this story because the Corinthians were doing something similar: eating and drinking in the presence of idols while claiming to belong to the true God. Spiritual experience does not make you immune to idolatry. It can happen in the shadow of the mountain.

storyConnections.title: The Bronze Serpent
storyConnections.summary: On the long journey around Edom the people grew impatient and spoke against God and Moses, complaining about the manna and asking why they had been brought into the wilderness to die. They were testing the Lord. And fiery serpents came among them, and many died. When the people confessed their sin, God told Moses to make a bronze serpent and set it on a pole, and everyone who had been bitten and looked at it lived. Paul uses the first half of the story as a warning in 1 Corinthians 10:9: do not test the Lord. Jesus uses the second half as a picture of the gospel in John 3:14: as Moses lifted up the serpent, the Son of Man must be lifted up, so that whoever believes in Him should not perish. The same story contains both warning and salvation.

storyConnections.title: David on the Rooftop
storyConnections.summary: In the spring, when kings went out to battle, David stayed home in Jerusalem. One evening he got up from his bed and walked on the roof of his palace, and he saw a woman bathing. At that moment there were several ways of escape: he could have turned away, gone back inside, or gone out to join his army. Instead he sent to find out who she was. Even when he learned she was the wife of Uriah, one of his loyal soldiers, he could have stopped. He did not. He sent for her, slept with her, and then arranged her husband's death to cover his sin. David was a man after God's own heart, a man who thought he was standing. He fell because he walked past one door after another. When the prophet Nathan confronted him, David repented, and God forgave him — but the consequences followed his family for the rest of his life. The way of escape was there every step of the way.
